basis: The printing heads this quaestio 'VERS. 17.' and it opens '(Vers. 17.) Et cecidit Abraam super faciem suam, et risit: et dixit in corde suo, Si'. The printing's caput and the lemma's own words, matched against the Clementine, name the same chapter.
date_basis: Written at Bethlehem and named in Jerome's own De viris illustribus 135, finished in 393, among the works already published; the preface announces it as the first of a series of Hebrew Questions on the whole of Scripture that he never continued. The early 390s is as close as the evidence held here reaches. The date is the writing, not the 1845 printing and not Vallarsi's 1767 edition.
text: (Vers. 17.) Et cecidit Abraam super faciem suam, et risit: et dixit in corde suo, Si centenario nascetur filius, et Sara nonagenaria pariet? Et post paululum: Et vocabis nomen ejus Isaac. Diversa opinio, sed una est etymologia, quare appellatus sit Isaac. Interpretatur enim Isaac, risus. Alii dicunt, quod Sara riserit, ideo eum risum vocatum esse, quod falsum est. Alii vero quod riserit Abraham, quod et nos probamus. Postquam enim ad risum Abrahae, vocatus est filius ejus Isaac, tunc legimus risisse et Saram. Sciendum tamen quod quatuor in veteri Testamento absque ullo velamine, nominibus suis antequam nascerentur, vocati sunt: Ismael, Isaac, Salomon, et Josias. Lege Scripturas.
